entries.text: probeHarness refused to arm on `get("worker")==="1"`. That is not a parse bug — both call sites parsed identically and correctly. It is a bug in the QUESTION: it needed "is the worker active?" and asked "does the URL literally say worker=1?". Those agree in todays regime and are OPPOSITE the moment the default flips, so the guard would have armed the instrument precisely when it was needed. The BACKLOG described the consequence BACKWARDS as refuse-by-default, i.e. benign. Lesson: a guard phrased against the spelling of an input silently stops tracking the state it guards when the default moves.

Two host INTENT apply paths exist and only one was worker-aware; the migration successor open-coded dispatch(world, stamped). No test could distinguish them because BOTH are correct today (a promoted host has a null driver). The divergence only becomes a bug in a regime that does not exist yet. Behavioural tests cannot see this class at all — it is a property of the call graph — so it is held by a source scan.

simWorkerDriver set `failed` ONLY from an explicit error event. A worker hanging WITHOUT throwing latched inFlight forever while isReady stayed true, freezing the game permanently and silently — and the direct-sim fallback could never fire, because the sole thing that arms it is the flag the hang cannot set. A recovery path is only real if the failure it recovers from can actually reach it.

isSimWorkerRequested takes an optional defaultOn so the suite pins BOTH regimes today. The inversion survived because every existing test exercised only the regime where the two questions agree. Verifying a flip BEFORE taking it requires exercising the post-flip regime, not the current one.

The gating red was on record as "CI throughput OR a real stall — unresolved". Both were wrong. `primitives.length > sampleA` is a strict-increase test on a NON-MONOTONIC counter: razePrimitives deletes entries and MID bots sever deliberately. One CI attempt sampled 33 and failed at 32 — BELOW its own sample. No timeout, retry, or faster runner could ever have made it pass. Before debugging an environment, check whether the assertion can be satisfied AT ALL.

One message covered dead page, unmet predicate, and out-of-runway. Three sessions could not choose between hypotheses because the instrument never distinguished them. The fix that mattered most was not the oracle — it was making the failure SAY which of the three it is, including saying outright when a signal must NOT be read as a product failure.

I built the growth oracle on nextPrimitiveId. It is HOST-ONLY and excluded from NetSnapshot, so on a worker mirror it is FROZEN — my new diagnostic printed "INSTRUMENT OK, PREDICATE GENUINELY UNMET: this is a real product failure" while the game was building normally. Caught only by dumping the state and seeing cursor 33 against a live primitive with id 38. An assertive diagnostic is not a correct one; I had written the very warning it violated one function above.

A full gating run reported 4 failures. I had edited src/state/workerSim.ts WHILE it executed against a live vite dev server, including a window where queuedOrderTotal was referenced before it existed. The clean rerun was 36/36. I nearly attributed 3 phantom regressions to my own correct changes — never run a suite and edit its sources concurrently, and treat an unexplained multi-failure jump as suspect first.

The guard that existed specifically to stop the wide compare being decorative added TEN family sizes and compared >0 — satisfied by any one. Measured: defenders 0 for all 300 frames while the guard sat green on poops. An aggregate assertion over N things proves something about the aggregate and nothing about any member; if the point is per-member coverage, the assertion must be per-member.

The first per-family table read the FINAL frame and failed on rainbows — 0, but only because a rainbow spawns and despawns mid-run, so it WAS compared on every frame it existed. A final-frame read under-reports every transient family. Now the PEAK across compared frames. The guard was right and my use of it was wrong, which is the good failure mode.

I added gathererOrders to structuralSignature citing its docblock about UNFORCED sites — then mutation-tested it and deleting BOTH terms left the entire suite green. My fix for a decorative site was decorative. Only after adding a test pinning the map-size term AND the depth term (a second enqueue leaves .size unchanged) did both mutations go red. Mutation-test the guard, never just the code.
